syllabus.clause: storage levels (memory/disk, serialised, replicated), LRU eviction and recomputation; cache keeps lineage while checkpoint (reliable) and localCheckpoint truncate it; when caching hurts (memory stolen from execution, cache of a non-deterministic plan).

at.step: Reveal: cached -- run one pays once, run two reuses it
Elaborate: why -- the cached data sits ready, unused computation behind it
Reveal: memory-only recomputes, memory-and-disk reads back
Elaborate: why -- the storage level decides what eviction costs you
Reveal: a non-deterministic answer, frozen once cached

items.item: without persist/cache, an action may recompute a transformed RDD from scratch; persist/cache keep it around for faster reuse next time

at.step: Reveal: the baseline -- uncached, both runs genuinely redo the work

items.item: cache() defaults to MEMORY_ONLY, which does not cache partitions that don't fit and recomputes them on the fly each time they're needed

at.step: Reveal: memory-only recomputes, memory-and-disk reads back

items.item: MEMORY_AND_DISK stores partitions that don't fit in memory on disk and reads them from there when needed, instead of recomputing

at.step: Reveal: memory-only recomputes, memory-and-disk reads back

sources.source: StorageLevel.scala (Apache Spark source, GitHub, tag v4.0.0)

items.item: a storage level is represented as independent flags -- use memory, use disk, deserialized, replication count -- confirming the documented levels are named combinations of the same four choices

at.step: Elaborate: why -- the storage level decides what eviction costs you

sources.source: ReliableCheckpointRDD.scala (Apache Spark source, GitHub, tag v4.0.0)

items.item: a reliable checkpoint's own RDD reads purely from checkpoint files on reliable storage, carrying no reference to the RDD it was checkpointed from

localCheckpoint() truncates lineage the same way reliable checkpoint() does, but writes to executor-local storage instead of reliable storage -- faster, but lost entirely if the executor holding the data dies, unlike a reliable checkpoint which survives executor loss. This topic's own examples.py measures cache's lineage-preserving recomputation/eviction behavior, not either checkpoint variant's own write path.

at.out: localCheckpoint's own local-vs-reliable trade-off named only, per the syllabus clause's own explicit mention; this topic's own examples.py does not measure either checkpoint variant directly

items.item: A non-deterministic plan cached partway through a job can silently produce different downstream results on retry: if a task reading the cached data fails after only some partitions were cached, Spark recomputes the missing partitions from the original (non-deterministic) computation, producing values that disagree with the partitions that were already cached successfully -- a correctness hazard distinct from this topic's own clean before/after cache contrast.

at.out: the partial-cache-plus-retry correctness hazard for a non-deterministic plan named only; this topic's own examples.py measures the simpler cached-vs-uncached contrast on a plan that fully materializes in one action

items.item: LRU is the eviction policy Spark's own MemoryStore uses when storage memory runs out and borrowed execution memory is reclaimed -- the least-recently-used cached block is dropped first, which is why a job with several differently-sized cached DataFrames doesn't necessarily lose the largest or newest one first.

at.out: LRU as the specific eviction policy named only; this topic's own examples.py forces eviction with a single large filler rather than distinguishing LRU from another policy across several cached blocks

items.item: Caching stealing execution memory from the rest of the job (rather than simply costing the memory it uses) is itself a form of the previous topic's own spill: a cache that claims storage memory under memory pressure can force a concurrently-running task's own sort or aggregation into spilling that it otherwise wouldn't have needed to.

at.out: caching-induced spill in a concurrently-running task named only, cross-referencing the previous topic's own spill mechanics; this topic's own examples.py measures caching's recomputation/eviction behavior in isolation, not its knock-on effect on a sibling task's spill

items.item: Spark also automatically persists some intermediate shuffle data (e.g. the map output of a shuffle) even without the user calling persist, specifically so a node failure during the shuffle doesn't force recomputing the entire input -- a distinct, automatic form of the same underlying idea this topic's own examples.py measures only as an explicit, user-chosen cache() or persist() call.

at.out: Spark's own automatic shuffle-output persistence named only; this topic's own examples.py measures only explicit, user-requested caching

items.item: Serialized storage levels (MEMORY_ONLY_SER, MEMORY_AND_DISK_SER) trade more CPU on read for a smaller memory footprint than the deserialized default -- a third axis (serialized vs. not) independent of the memory-vs-disk axis this topic's own examples.py measures directly.

at.out: the serialized-vs-deserialized storage-level axis named only; this topic's own examples.py measures only the memory-vs-disk eviction axis, using the deserialized default

items.item: Replicated storage levels (MEMORY_ONLY_2, etc.) trade cache memory for faster fault recovery -- if one executor holding a replica dies, Spark can read the surviving replica instead of recomputing the lost partition at all, a third strategy beyond 'recompute' and 'spill to disk' for surviving data loss.

at.out: replicated storage levels as a third survival strategy named only; this topic's own examples.py measures the simpler recompute-vs-disk-spill contrast without replication

items.item: unpersist() explicitly releases a cached dataset's own storage immediately, rather than waiting for LRU eviction under pressure or garbage collection of the DataFrame reference -- the deliberate, intentional counterpart to the involuntary eviction this topic's own second claim measures as happening under memory pressure instead.

at.out: unpersist()'s own deliberate, immediate release named only, as the counterpart to the eviction this topic measures; this topic's own examples.py isolates its three scenarios with separate SparkSessions rather than exercising unpersist() as a measured claim

items.item: checkpoint() requires a checkpoint directory to be set on the SparkContext first (setCheckpointDir), and is itself eager, not lazy -- calling it immediately triggers a job that writes the data out, unlike cache()/persist(), which only mark an RDD for caching and materialize it lazily on the next action.

at.out: checkpoint()'s own eager-materialization behavior and its setCheckpointDir precondition named only; this topic's own examples.py measures cache()'s lazy materialization, not checkpoint()'s eager one

items.item: In PySpark specifically, cached objects are always serialized through the Pickle library regardless of which storage level is chosen, so the serialized-vs-deserialized axis that matters in Scala/Java is largely invisible from the Python API -- a language-specific wrinkle on top of the storage-level axis this topic's own examples.py measures in Python throughout.

at.out: PySpark's own always-Pickle serialization behavior named only, sourced directly from the RDD Programming Guide's own note; this topic's own examples.py runs entirely in PySpark, where this wrinkle applies to every measured scenario
